Squared correlation of the predicted shocks with the true shocks

Source: R/prediction_corr.R
prediction_corr.Rd

Computes the population squared correlation between the shocks predicted by predict_shocks() and the true underlying shocks, as a measure of the precision of the prediction (Burri and Kaufmann, 2026a).

Usage

prediction_corr(Psi, SigR, Sig = NULL, squared = TRUE)

Arguments

Psi

Numeric matrix (M x E) of responses of the residuals to the E structural shocks (e.g. Psi from hetiv()).

SigR

Numeric matrix (M x M). Covariance matrix of the residuals on control (non-event) days.

Sig

Numeric matrix (M x M) or NULL. Covariance matrix of the residuals on event days, used to rescale Psi to one-standard-deviation shocks. If NULL (default), Psi is assumed to be in these units already.

squared

Logical. If TRUE (default), the squared correlation is returned. If FALSE, its square root (the correlation).

Value

A numeric vector of length E with the squared correlation between each predicted shock and the true shock (the diagonal of S (I + S)^{-1}), or the correlation if squared = FALSE.

Details

Let the residuals on event days be e_t = Psi eps_t + v_t, with unit-variance shocks eps_t and non-policy noise v_t with covariance SigR. The linear prediction of the shocks has covariance with the true shocks S (I + S)^{-1}, with the signal-to-noise matrix S = Psi' SigR^{-1} Psi. The diagonal of this matrix is the share of the shock variance explained by the prediction (one minus the relative mean squared error), that is, the squared correlation between the predicted and the true shock.

The correlation itself does not depend on the units of the shocks, but the formula does: S is the signal-to-noise ratio only if Psi is the response to a one-standard-deviation shock. The estimators return Psi normalised to a unit impact response instead, which leaves the variance of the shocks out of S. If Sig is supplied, the columns of Psi are therefore rescaled by the implied standard deviations of the shocks, recovered from Sig - SigR in the same way as in predict_shocks(). If Sig is NULL, Psi is used as is.

The measure is a population quantity evaluated at the estimated parameters. It does not account for estimation error in Psi, Sig and SigR, and it is informative only if the responses in Psi are consistently estimated, that is, if the identifying assumptions of the estimator hold.

The measure also requires a nonsingular covariance SigR. If fewer non-policy shocks than variables drive the data, SigR is (nearly) singular, the implied signal-to-noise ratio becomes very large and the measure approaches one whatever the actual precision. A warning is issued in this case.

References

Burri, M. and Kaufmann, D. (2026a). Measuring monetary policy shocks. IRENE Working Papers 24-03, IRENE Institute of Economic Research, University of Neuchatel.

See also

predict_shocks()

Examples

# One shock with unit variance, two variables
Psi <- matrix(c(1, 0.5), nrow = 2)
SigR <- diag(c(0.5, 0.5))
prediction_corr(Psi, SigR)
#> [1] 0.7142857

# Psi normalised to unit impact; the shock has variance 4
Sig <- SigR + 4 * Psi %*% t(Psi)
prediction_corr(Psi, SigR, Sig = Sig)
#> [1] 0.9090909
